newsitem.title: UK: Exit polls show Labour landslide in UK election.
newsitem.headline: Exit polls show Labour landslide in UK election.

text.p: Tony Blair's Labour party is poised to sweep to power for the first time since 1979 in a landslide victory not seen in 150 years, according to exit polls released on Thursday as voting ended in Britain's election.

The polls, conducted by Britain's two main television news broadcasters, BBC and ITN, said Labour was likely to have a huge majority in parliament, ending 18 years of Conservative rule that has transformed Britain.

ITN projected that Labour would have a majority of 159 seats in the 659-seat House of Commons. The BBC, whose polls gave Labour 47 percent support with 29 percent for the Conservatives, said the majoirty could be nearer to 200.
"Tonight represents a truly seismic shift," Jonathan Dimbleby, presenting ITN's programme, said.
"After losing four times, just to win is important. It looks as if we are going to win in very good fashion indeed," John Prescott, Labour's deputy leader, told BBC television.
Despite the ominous signs, Conservative party chairman Brian Mawhinney refused to concede defeat.
"I am saying the people have already decided. We will wait until that judgement becomes clear, and we will accept that judgement," he told BBC television.
The first actual results will not start to come in until around 2300 GMT, two hours after the last of Britain's 44 million eligible voters cast their ballots.
A record 3,717 candidates are standing for 659 seats, eight more than in 1992 because of boundary changes.
Polling officials reported that turnout was brisk across the country on the warmest day of the year so far.
Security was heavy to combat any attempt by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to disprupt the voting as it has done during the six-week campaign with a string of bombs and hoaxes.

Opinion polls published during the campaign, the longest this century, pointed to a landslide victory for Labour, which has dumped its socialist ideology and methodically wooed middle-class voters since Tony Blair became its leader in 1994.

Blair, 43, would be the youngest prime minister this century if the exit polls, which asked people how they actually voted, prove to be accurate. He was a student at Oxford University when Labour last won a British election in 1974.
Defeat for Prime Minister John Major, who defied polls to come from behind to win the 1992 election, would be the end of an era in British politics.

Over 18 years, first under "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher and then under Major, the Conservatives turned Britain upside down, halting decades of relative economic decline by privatising vast swathes of industry, taming powerful trade unions and making it easier for firms to hire and fire workers.

But critics said the price of greater economic efficiency was too high, with crime and homelessness rising and the gap between rich and poor widening more than in any other developed country except New Zealand.

In the course of a gruelling but largely uneventful campaign, Blair hammered home his argument that Britain had become a less fair, less decent society and promised to turn it into a country "for the many, not the few".
Major's appeal to voters was "better the devil you know than the devil you don't".

Major acknowledged past mistakes, including Britain's humiliating ejection from the European Union's currency grid in 1992, but urged voters not to turn their backs on a party that was now delivering an economic boom.
